To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the instantaneous power of a circuit is the sum of the Joule losses and the energy stored/restores in the circuit elements and that the instantaneous power can be computed from the voltage and current at circuit terminals.

(1) the instantaneous power P(t) is the sum of the active power (or real power) P_r(t) and the reactive power P_x(t), (2) the active power is equal to the Joule losses in resistors plus the hystereses losses in magnetic elements, (3) the reactive power is the difference between the energy stored/restoried in magnetic elements and the energy dissipated in capacitors, (4) the instantaneous power is equal to zero for

(i) the power components of magnetic saturating circuits are the same as those of switching circuits (active, reactive, and distortion power); and (ii) the power components for magnetic hysteretic circuits are the same except for the reactive power, which is the sum of two components: the reactive power of a linear circuit and the power consumed by the hysteresic loop of the magnetic element.

the theoretical foundations of electrical power theory, and we have developed a new method for the identification of power components in general single-phase magnetic nonlinear circuits.
the development of a general power theory for nonlinear circuits that is applicable to all types of circuits and that is consistent with the laws of physics.
the theoretical foundations of the power theory and its application in the analysis and design of power electronic systems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the instantaneous power of any circuit is the sum of three power components: the active power (P) which represents the Joule losses in all resistive and inductors, the stored/ restored power (Q) which represents the energy stored/restor ed by magnetic elements and the hysteresic power (W) which represents the losses in the hysteric loops.

the power components of any nonlinear circuit, including magnetic elements with saturation and hystersis, are correctly identified from the Poynting theorem, and that the instantaneous active, reactive, and apparent powers, as well as the instantaneous power components, can be computed from only the instantaneous voltage and currents.
the instantaneous active and reactive powers defined in the literature are not the same, but rather they are the same only when the circuit contains only resistive and linear inductive elements.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, the Poynting theorem is a useful tool to correctly identify the power components of magnetic saturating and hysteretic circuits, which is not possible with other methods.
the active and reactive power components of a single-phase circuit can be identified by computing the average values of the Poynting vector at the terminals.

the Poynting theorem provides a general and powerful tool for power theory, which is capable of identifying all the power components in a general nonlinear circuit, including magnetic elements with nonlinear B-H curves.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the active power component is always the power that is delivered to the circuit, and the reactive power component is always that power which is delivered back to the source.
the Poynting theorem provides a powerful tool for computing the power components of a circuit from only the terminal voltage and current waveforms.
the active power is always the energy consumed in the circuit elements, while the reactive power is the energy stored/restores in the circuit elements.
